response_text:
===FINDING 1===
LEAD: Recorded spending on 5,630 costed activities was Rs 51.96 crore below planned cost across the 20-Gram-Panchayat sample. The shortfall is spread across blocks and almost every asset category, rather than being confined to one type of work.
DETAIL: Rangeilunda and Kalimela warrant first attention: Rangeilunda recorded Rs 2.73 crore spent against Rs 11.84 crore planned, a gap of Rs 9.11 crore and 23.1% utilisation; Kalimela recorded Rs 1.76 crore against Rs 7.65 crore, a gap of Rs 5.90 crore and 23.0% utilisation. The broad pattern holds for 27 of 28 category groupings across the 16 sampled blocks; Banking Facilities showed no clear pattern. At the next review, ask these blocks to reconcile planned costs with work status and recorded payments, and establish whether the gaps reflect delayed execution, incomplete expenditure entries or revised plans—the data alone does not identify the cause.

===FINDING 1===
LEAD: Costed activities in the 20-GP sample show a combined gap of Rs 51.96 crore between planned cost and recorded spending. The gap is spread across all 16 blocks and nearly every asset category, rather than being confined to one block.
DETAIL: The largest block-level gaps are in Rangeilunda, where Rs 2.73 crore was spent against Rs 11.84 crore planned, and Kalimela, where Rs 1.76 crore was spent against Rs 7.65 crore planned. Even the smaller cited gaps reflect utilisation below 53%; only Banking Facilities showed no clear distribution pattern. Blocks should reconcile older plans with expenditure and current work status, but the data alone cannot distinguish delayed works, unspent plans or incomplete payment records.

===FINDING 4===
LEAD: For activities with sanction records, recorded spending is Rs 5.02 crore below the sanctioned amount across the nine sampled districts. This is a widespread gap across almost every asset category, not an issue attributable to one district alone.
DETAIL: Ganjam has the largest cited gap, with Rs 4.61 crore spent against Rs 6.30 crore sanctioned, followed by Khordha with Rs 3.33 crore spent against Rs 4.06 crore; Cuttack is closer at Rs 2.14 crore of Rs 2.33 crore. Banking Facilities was the only category without a clear pattern. Because only about one in six activities has a sanction record, these are not programme-wide utilisation rates; districts should first reconcile missing sanctions and then review ageing sanctioned balances.

===FINDING 5===
LEAD: Two undescribed output codes account for 92.2% of the Rs 56.20 crore in planned untied funding for public works. Until these codes are defined, officers cannot tell what most of this discretionary funding is intended to deliver.
DETAIL: Code 101 accounts for Rs 34.88 crore and Code 105 for Rs 16.90 crore, and they lead in 19 of the 20 sampled GPs; Haldikudar follows a different pattern. As none of the eight output codes has a description on file, the next review should obtain the code definitions, verify Haldikudar’s coding and confirm that activities have been assigned to the intended outputs.

===FINDING 7===
LEAD: More than half of public works—5,181 of 9,418, or 55%—have no asset category recorded. This data gap is the largest category in 19 of the 20 sampled GPs and limits meaningful review of what the works are creating.
DETAIL: Govindapur is the only GP with a different leading category. By comparison, Buildings, the largest named category, contains 688 activities. GPs should complete or correct asset classifications, starting with the uncategorised records and checking whether Govindapur’s different pattern reflects better data entry or a genuinely different works portfolio.

===FINDING 8===
LEAD: Activities still recorded as “Activity Approved” account for Rs 41.61 crore of the Rs 51.96 crore gap between planned cost and spending. Only Rs 14 lakh is recorded as spent against their Rs 41.75 crore planned cost.
DETAIL: This status has the largest plan-to-spending gap in 18 of the 20 sampled GPs; no clear pattern was found in Boipariguda or Laxmipur. Abandoned works also show only Rs 21.03 lakh spent against Rs 5.85 crore planned, while ongoing works have used 85.4% of planned cost. Officials should age the approved and abandoned records, verify whether works have actually progressed, and update stale statuses or missing payments; the figures do not by themselves establish delay or non-performance.

===FINDING 10===
LEAD: Rs 28.59 crore, or 93.9%, of all recorded spending from the General social-category component is attached to works still marked “WORK ONGOING.” This concentration warrants a check on whether completed works and their statuses are being updated promptly.
DETAIL: Ongoing works account for the majority of this spending in 18 of the 20 sampled GPs; Boipariguda and Laxmipur show no clear pattern. A further Rs 1.15 crore is attached to abandoned works. Review teams should reconcile work status with vouchers, completion records and photo evidence, while noting that these figures cover only the General component and not total expenditure across all social-category components.

===FINDING 12===
LEAD: Almost all recorded expected beneficiaries—2,03,534 of 2,06,929, or 98.4%—are attached to activities still marked “Activity Approved.” Completed activities record no expected beneficiaries, pointing to a likely status or beneficiary-data gap that needs reconciliation.
DETAIL: “Activity Approved” has the highest expected-beneficiary count in 18 of the 20 sampled GPs; Boipariguda and Laxmipur show no clear pattern. Beneficiary information exists for only 763 activities, so this cannot establish how many people were actually served. GPs should verify statuses and complete expected and actual beneficiary records, especially for ongoing and completed activities.

===FINDING 13===
LEAD: Half of all planned untied funding for costed activities—Rs 30.07 crore of Rs 59.64 crore—is assigned to “Self-sufficient Infrastructure in Village.” This is the leading theme in 18 of the 20 sampled GPs.
DETAIL: Kalimela instead gives the largest share to “Water Sufficient Village,” while Boipariguda’s largest amount is under “Unmapped theme.” Across the sample, Rs 5.70 crore is unmapped, so Boipariguda’s focus-area mappings should be corrected or confirmed; Kalimela should be asked to explain its different priority mix. These figures describe planned discretionary funding, not actual spending.

===FINDING 14===
LEAD: Code 101 accounts for a Rs 2.49 crore gap between sanctioned and spent amounts for New/Fresh works, and has the largest such gap in 19 of the 20 sampled Gram Panchayats.
DETAIL: Code 101 recorded Rs 14.94 crore spent against Rs 17.43 crore sanctioned, or 85.7% utilisation. Chikilli showed no clear pattern. Because output codes 101–110 have no descriptions and sanctions are recorded for only about one in six activities, officials should first obtain the code definitions and reconcile Code 101 sanctions, expenditure and work status rather than treat the gap as confirmed non-performance.

===FINDING 15===
LEAD: All 6,893 geotagged photo uploads recorded for New/Fresh works are attached to Code 101, although that code represents only 32.8% of the activities in scope.
DETAIL: Codes 102, 103, 109 and 110 have no photo uploads recorded, and the concentration in Code 101 appears across 19 of the 20 sampled Gram Panchayats; Chikilli has no clear pattern. As none of the output codes has a description on file, check whether photo evidence is being linked or classified incorrectly before concluding that works under the other codes lack evidence.

===FINDING 17===
LEAD: Codes 101 and 105 have the largest gaps between planned cost and recorded spending across every beneficiary-purpose group in the sample.
DETAIL: Code 101 shows Rs 15.88 crore spent against Rs 46.85 crore planned, while Code 105 shows Rs 7.32 crore against Rs 22.43 crore; their utilisation of planned cost is 33.9% and 32.6%, respectively. The pattern holds for General, SC, ST and all/general-public activities, but the undefined output codes and different activity volumes limit interpretation; reviews should identify what these codes represent and check the age and status of the underlying works.

===FINDING 18===
LEAD: Almost all tied funding in the sampled costed activities is planned for sanitation and drinking water: Rs 8.82 crore and Rs 8.42 crore, respectively.
DETAIL: Sanitation receives 49.9% and drinking water 47.7% of the Rs 17.66 crore tied-fund total, and both lead across every beneficiary-purpose group. Roads are a distant third at Rs 31.01 lakh. This may reflect the permitted purposes of tied grants rather than a planning imbalance, but officials should verify that focus-area classifications are correct and that the allocations match local priorities and grant conditions.

===FINDING 19===
LEAD: Chikilli has no sanctioned amount recorded in any of the six years, despite accounting for 5.0% of the activities in this 20-GP sample.
DETAIL: Chikilli records Rs 0 in sanctions from 2020-21 through 2025-26, whereas the sample total is Rs 28.84 crore and the next-lowest GP, Govindapur, records Rs 99.78 lakh. Sanction data exists for only about one in six activities, so this does not establish that Chikilli received no approvals; the priority is to check for missing sanction records, failed activity links or a different recording practice.

===FINDING 21===
LEAD: Rs 1.02 crore of General-category spending is classified under “Other” grant components rather than Tied or Untied, and this remains the smallest category in every year.
DETAIL: “Other” represents 3.6% of the Rs 28.48 crore in voucher-linked General-category spending, compared with Rs 16.75 crore under Untied and Rs 10.71 crore under Tied. The label covers any component outside the standard tied and untied codes and does not by itself indicate an error; officials should identify the components included and reconcile any miscoded or unexplained entries.

===FINDING 22===
LEAD: Recorded statuses may need substantial updating: 10,108 of the 12,704 activities remain at “Activity Approved”, while only 17 are marked completed.
DETAIL: A further 2,110 activities are recorded as ongoing and 420 as abandoned, with the same broad ordering across all six financial years. These are database statuses and do not prove that works remain unfinished; blocks should review older approved and ongoing entries, confirm action on abandoned works, and correct the 13 records where “Buildings” has been entered as a status.

LEAD: Activity-linked expenditure in the 20-GP sample shows a broad upward trend, reaching Rs 5.92 crore in 2025-26 compared with Rs 42.43 lakh in 2020-21.
DETAIL: The upward pattern appears whether the records are viewed by month, quarter or fiscal year, although it is not a continuous year-on-year rise: expenditure fell to Rs 3.66 crore in 2023-24 before increasing again. ===FINDING 6===
LEAD: Bhubaneswar Block accounts for one-quarter of all payment vouchers in the sample and recorded the highest count in five of the six years reviewed.
DETAIL: Bhubaneswar recorded 2,135 of 8,529 vouchers, well ahead of Rangeilunda at 945 and Bheden at 885. The only exception was 2024-25, when no block had a clear lead; review whether Bhubaneswar’s consistently high volume is explained by the number and activity of sampled GPs or by a different voucher-recording practice.
===FINDING 9===
LEAD: Payment-voucher recording follows a recurring cycle at monthly and quarterly levels, suggesting that workload may be concentrated at predictable points in the reporting calendar.
DETAIL: No comparable pattern is visible across fiscal years, whose totals range from 1,003 vouchers in 2023-24 to 1,985 in 2025-26. Review the monthly and quarterly peaks to determine whether they reflect genuine payment schedules or bunching and delayed entry of vouchers; the pattern alone cannot distinguish between these explanations.
===FINDING 11===
LEAD: Activity-linked expenditure is generally rising by quarter in six of the nine sampled districts, but Bargarh, Koraput and Cuttack do not follow that direction and merit separate review.
DETAIL: The rising pattern appears in Khordha, Ganjam, Kandhamal, Sundargarh, Malkangiri and Rayagada. Across the sample, several first quarters were among the highest—including Rs 1.99 crore in 2026-Q1—so ask the three exception districts whether their different trajectories reflect work timing, payment posting, incomplete activity links or local implementation conditions.
===FINDING 16===
LEAD: Most cashbook measures show a recurring annual cycle, while activity-linked expenditure follows a shorter three-month cycle and sanction records behave differently.
DETAIL: Payment and receipt amounts, voucher counts, and average monthly inflows and outflows per GP all repeat on a roughly 12-month cycle. Activity-linked expenditure instead repeats about every three months, while sanction counts and amounts show other patterns; compare peak months with sanction, execution and reporting calendars to check whether these cycles reflect programme operations or periodic data entry.
===FINDING 20===
LEAD: Districts show markedly different timing patterns in activity-linked expenditure, so a single quarterly monitoring expectation may not fit the whole sample.
DETAIL: Khordha, Bargarh, Ganjam, Koraput and Cuttack show a cycle repeating about every 12 quarters; Sundargarh’s repeats about every six quarters and Rayagada’s about every three, while Kandhamal and Malkangiri follow other patterns. Review whether these differences are supported by work and fund-release schedules or indicate inconsistent timing of payment-to-activity linking; the detected cycles do not by themselves establish a problem.
===FINDING 23===
LEAD: Receipt-voucher recording is cyclical within months and quarters, while annual receipt counts have generally fallen from 816 in 2020-21 to 565 in 2025-26.
DETAIL: The monthly and quarterly series show a recurring 12-step cycle, but fiscal years follow a different pattern; annual counts reached their lowest level at 555 in 2024-25 before a small rise. Check whether receipts are being consolidated into fewer vouchers, received less frequently, or entered in batches, since voucher counts alone do not show the value of funds received.
===FINDING 24===
LEAD: The number of sanctions is rising at quarterly and annual levels, reaching 485 in 2025-26 compared with 155 in 2020-21.
DETAIL: The monthly records follow a different pattern, so the overall increase may coexist with irregular or concentrated sanction issuance during the year. Review whether staffing and implementation capacity are keeping pace with the higher sanction volume and whether monthly bunching is linked to approval schedules or delayed entry.
===FINDING 26===
LEAD: Activity-linked expenditure is rising by quarter in nine of the 16 sampled blocks, while seven blocks follow different trajectories that should be reviewed individually.
DETAIL: The upward pattern appears in Bhubaneswar, Khallikote, Khajuripada, Lahunipara, Kalimela, Kalyansingpur, Balisankara, Laxmipur and Sheragada. Barpali, Bheden, Rangeilunda, Boipariguda, Baranga, Tangi Choudwar and Attabira are the exceptions; ask whether their patterns reflect execution schedules, payment timing or gaps in linking cashbook payments to planned activities rather than assuming weaker performance.

LEAD: Ganjam’s cashbook activity changes sharply around August 2020, while sanctions and activity-linked expenditure shift later, in October and November respectively.
DETAIL: Payment and receipt amounts, voucher counts, and average monthly inflows and outflows per GP all show a statistical break in August 2020; sanction counts and amounts break in October, and activity-linked expenditure in November. The analysis does not show whether these were increases or decreases, so reconcile records around these months and check for programme starts, data-system changes, back-entry or other administrative events before drawing conclusions.

DETAIL: Bhubaneswar recorded Rs 3.26 crore over the six years, although the annual path was uneven: expenditure rose to Rs 74.21 lakh in 2022-23, fell to Rs 30.60 lakh in 2023-24 and then recovered. Barpali nevertheless leads in activity-linked expenditure, sanction count and sanctioned amount, so reconcile sanctions, planned works and cashbook payments to understand whether this reflects implementation timing, differences in activity linking or the composition of sampled GPs.
===FINDING 32===
LEAD: During 2024-25, the average monthly cashbook outflow per sampled GP showed an upward pattern across months and quarters; the full-year average was Rs 3.99 lakh per GP-month.
DETAIL: A fiscal-year trend cannot be assessed because only 2024-25 is included in this finding, with the annual average based on 240 GP-month records. Review the monthly and quarterly increase for possible year-end concentration, delayed posting or a genuine acceleration in payments, rather than interpreting it as a multi-year rise.
